summary: Defines an SDP cryptographic attribute for unicast media streams. The attribute carries a cryptographic key and other parameters to configure security for the stream in a single message or one round trip, and can be used with various transport protocols. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC adds one line to a session description that says which encryption and authentication to use for a media stream and carries the key itself. The point of putting the key in the description is that both ends can start a secure call in a single exchange instead of running a separate key exchange first.

questions: what is the sdp crypto attribute
how does srtp key exchange work in sdp
subtitle: How the key for an encrypted media stream is put into the session description, so both sides can set up SRTP in one exchange.

tldr.problem: SDP could say that a call uses secure RTP, but it had no way to say which algorithm to use or which key to use, so the two ends had to fall back on defaults.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a media-level SDP attribute called crypto, which carries a tag, a crypto-suite name, the keying material and optional session parameters. Each end sends its own key, so both directions of the call are protected.
tldr.outcome: The attribute is meant for two-party unicast streams, and the RFC insists that the SDP message carrying the key must itself be protected by something such as TLS, IPsec or S/MIME.

facts.label: Attribute format
facts.value: a=crypto: then tag, crypto-suite, key-params and optional session-params

facts.label: KDR values
facts.value: 1 to 24, denoting a power of two

today: RFC 4568 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It defines the SDP crypto attribute and the SRTP-specific parameters, and it registers the crypto attribute, the inline key method, the SRTP transport, three crypto suites and the SRTP session parameters with IANA.

sections.title: Why a Crypto Attribute
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol describes multimedia sessions, which can be audio, video, whiteboard, fax, modem and other media streams. Security services such as data origin authentication, integrity and confidentiality are often needed for those streams. The Secure Real-time Transport Protocol provides security services for RTP media, and is signalled by using a secure RTP transport such as RTP/SAVP or RTP/SAVPF in an SDP media line. But there were no means within SDP itself to configure SRTP beyond using default values.

This RFC specifies a new SDP attribute called crypto, used to signal and negotiate cryptographic parameters for media streams in general and for SRTP in particular. The definition is limited to two-party unicast media streams where each source has a unique cryptographic key; multicast and multipoint unicast are left for further study.

The attribute is defined in a generic way so that it can be used with SRTP and with any other secure transport that can establish cryptographic parameters in a single message or a single round trip using the offer/answer model. Each type of secure media transport needs its own specification for the attribute's parameters, because those definitions are often unique to the transport, and each must be registered with IANA. This document defines the security parameters and keying material for SRTP only.

The RFC is explicit that this is not a replacement for a key management protocol. Sending a key over a medium where an attacker can read it, change its definition, or alter the parameters of the session is pointless, so the SDP security descriptions are suitable only for restricted cases where IPsec, TLS or some other encapsulating data security protocol protects the SDP message. In SIP, the application should use either the SIPS URI or S/MIME for that protection, and the use of transport layer or IP layer security instead is not recommended, because the protection cannot be ensured through intermediate entities such as SIP proxies.
sections.plainLanguage: Session descriptions are exchanged when a call starts, and they already say what media will be sent. This RFC uses the same moment to agree the encryption key, which saves a second exchange, but only if the description itself is protected on the way.

sections.title: The Crypto Attribute
sections.content:
A new media-level SDP attribute called crypto describes the cryptographic suite, key parameters and session parameters for the preceding unicast media line. It must appear only at the media level, not at the session level, and it has the form a=crypto:<tag> <crypto-suite> <key-params> [<session-params>]. The values of the fields are case-insensitive, although the attribute name itself is case-sensitive, and implementers are encouraged to use the case shown in the document.

The tag is a decimal number identifying a particular crypto attribute, and it must be unique among all crypto attributes for a given media line. Leading zeroes must not be used. With the offer/answer model the tag is a negotiated parameter, and it is how the offerer learns which of several offered attributes the answerer chose.

The crypto-suite is an identifier for the encryption and authentication algorithms used for the transport in question. Each transport defines its own set of possible values, so the same name may be reused for another transport but would need a separate definition. The crypto-suite is also a negotiated parameter.

The key parameters provide one or more sets of keying material, written as a method indicator, a colon, and the keying information. Only one method is defined in this document, namely inline, meaning the keying material is in the attribute itself. The method name is transport independent, while the meaning of the key information is specific to the transport and the method. When several keys are included, it must be possible to tell from the packet alone which key is in use; a trial-and-error approach is not allowed.

Session parameters are specific to a given transport and their use is optional. In the offer/answer model they may be negotiated, which means they apply to data sent in both directions, or declarative, which means they apply only to media sent by the entity that generated the description. A declarative parameter in an offer applies to media sent by the offerer; in an answer it applies to media sent by the answerer.

IANA has registered the attribute with the long form name 'Security description cryptographic attribute for media streams', as a media-level attribute not subject to charset, whose purpose is security descriptions.
sections.plainLanguage: The attribute has four parts: a number that identifies this particular line, the name of the algorithm, the key, and any extra settings. It is written inside a session description, after the media line it applies to.

sections.title: Using the Attribute With Offer and Answer
sections.content:
When generating an initial offer for a unicast stream, there must be one or more crypto attributes for each media stream for which security is desired, and each must have a unique tag. The order matters: the most preferred crypto line is listed first, and a more preferred crypto-suite should be cryptographically stronger than a less preferred one.

The crypto-suite always applies to media in the directions the media stream supports. The keys are different: they apply to the packets that the party which generated the description will send. Each endpoint therefore determines its own transmission keys and sends those keys to the other endpoint, and the recipient uses them to decrypt. The reason for this is consistency, and the fact that secure RTCP still flows in both directions even for a unidirectional stream.

The answerer must either accept exactly one of the offered crypto attributes or reject the offered stream. It should pick the most preferred attribute it can support, and only attributes that are valid may be accepted. The answer must contain the tag and crypto-suite of the accepted attribute, and the keys the answerer will use for media sent to the offerer; a key must be provided whatever direction attributes appear in the offer or answer. Negotiated session parameters must be included in the answer, while declarative parameters provided by the offerer are not, though the answerer may supply its own.

The offerer checks that one of the crypto suites it offered, with its tag, was accepted and echoed, and that the answer includes one or more keys. If any of that fails, the negotiation fails.

Outside the offer/answer model there is no negotiation of the crypto suite, key or session parameters: the sender determines them, must include exactly one crypto attribute, and the receiver must either accept it or should not receive the associated stream.

One backwards-compatibility case matters. The answerer may support the secure transport and accept the stream but not support the crypto attribute and ignore it. The offerer recognizes this by seeing an accepted stream in the answer with no crypto line, and the security negotiation must then fail.
sections.plainLanguage: The caller lists the ways it is willing to encrypt, best first, along with its own key. The callee picks one of them and replies with its own key. Each end then has the key it needs for the media it receives.

sections.title: The SRTP Key Parameter
sections.content:
For SRTP the inline key method carries the keying material, the master key and salt, and the policy attached to that master key, including how long it may be used and whether it uses a master key identifier to associate an incoming packet with a particular key. Compliant implementations obey those policies and must not accept packets that violate them, for example after the master key lifetime has expired.

The key parameter may contain one or more cryptographic master keys, each of which must be a unique cryptographically random value with respect to the other master keys in the whole SDP message, including those for other streams. Each key has the form inline: <key||salt> ["|" lifetime] ["|" MKI ":" length], where the key and salt are concatenated and then base64 encoded, the lifetime is the maximum number of SRTP or SRTCP packets that may use the master key, and the MKI and its length are the master key identifier and the size of the MKI field in the SRTP packet. The length of the concatenated key and salt is fixed by the crypto-suite; if the decoded length does not match, the crypto attribute must be treated as invalid.

The lifetime may be written as a decimal integer or as a power of two, using the literal '2^', and it must not exceed the maximum packet lifetime for the crypto-suite. The MKI is a positive decimal integer, and its length must be given; if the length is missing or greater than 128 bytes, the crypto attribute must be considered invalid. When a key parameter holds more than one master key, all of them must include an MKI value, and the MKI length must be the same for all keys in a given crypto attribute.

The specification deliberately does not support SRTP's other way of expressing a key lifetime, the pair of values called From and To, because the lifetime of an AES master key is 2^48 SRTP packets, so there is no cryptographic reason to replace a master key for practical point-to-point applications.
sections.plainLanguage: The key line holds the secret key and its salt, written in base64 so it can travel inside text. It can also say how many packets that key may be used for, and give the key an identifier so that a receiver can tell which of several keys a packet used.

sections.title: The Crypto-Suites
sections.content:
The SRTP crypto-suites define the encryption and authentication transforms used for the media stream. Three are defined. AES_CM_128_HMAC_SHA1_80 is the SRTP default: AES in counter mode with HMAC-SHA1 message authentication and an 80-bit authentication tag. AES_CM_128_HMAC_SHA1_32 is identical except that the authentication tag is 32 bits. F8_128_HMAC_SHA1_80 is identical to the first except that the cipher is F8.

All three share the same lengths. The master key is 128 bits and the master salt 112 bits. The default lifetime is a maximum of 2^48 SRTP packets or 2^31 SRTCP packets, whichever comes first. The encryption key is 128 bits, the message authentication code is HMAC-SHA1, and the SRTP and SRTCP authentication key lengths are 160 bits. The SRTP authentication tag is 80 bits in two of the suites and 32 bits in the third, while the SRTCP authentication tag is 80 bits in all three. The length of the base64-decoded key and salt must be 30 octets, that is 240 bits, for each of the suites, or the crypto attribute is considered invalid.

The RFC notes that although SRTP allows that many packets, automated key management should allow easy and efficient rekeying at intervals far smaller than 2^31 packets, given today's media rates.
sections.plainLanguage: Three ready-made combinations of algorithms are defined. They differ only in the cipher or in the length of the check that is attached to each packet, so choosing one is mostly a matter of how much overhead the application can accept.

sections.title: Session Parameters
sections.content:
Session parameters optionally override the SRTP defaults for the session. KDR gives the key derivation rate, the rate at which a pseudo-random function is applied to the master key; its value must be a decimal integer in the set 1 to 24, denoting a power of two from 2^1 to 2^24, and when it is omitted a single initial key derivation is performed. UNENCRYPTED_SRTP and UNENCRYPTED_SRTCP say that those payloads are not encrypted; if UNENCRYPTED_SRTCP is signalled then the SRTCP E bit must be clear in all SRTCP messages, and by default all SRTCP messages are encrypted and the E bit must be set. UNAUTHENTICATED_SRTP says that SRTP messages are not authenticated, and its use is not recommended, because the SRTP specification requires message authentication for SRTCP but not for SRTP.

FEC_ORDER signals the use of forward error correction for the RTP packets and takes the value FEC_SRTP or SRTP_FEC, which say whether the correction is applied before or after SRTP processing by the sender and the receiver; FEC_SRTP is the default. FEC_KEY gives separate master keys for a forward error correction stream sent to a different address or port, in exactly the same format as the SRTP key parameter, and it must not be given when the correction stream goes to the same address and port as the media stream, in which case the crypto attribute is invalid. WSH, the window size hint, is a hint for how large the replay protection window should be, whose minimum value in SRTP is 64.

New session parameters are mandatory by default, and one prefixed with a dash character is optional and may be ignored. An attribute received with an unknown session parameter that is not prefixed with a dash must be treated as invalid.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the switches that tune the protection for one session: how often a fresh key is derived from the master key, whether one direction is left in the clear, how the error correction is ordered, and how big the replay window should be.

sections.title: Setting Up the Cryptographic Context
sections.content:
Three pieces of information are critical to the operation of the default SRTP ciphers: the SSRC, the synchronization source; the ROC, the roll-over counter for a given SSRC; and the SEQ, the sequence number for a given SSRC. The RFC sets three constraints on them in a unicast session.

First, the keystream must be unique from other participants, because keystream reuse makes the ciphertext vulnerable to cryptanalysis: known plaintext in one stream can expose parts of the reused keystream and so expose more plaintext elsewhere. SRTP partly handles this by including the sender's SSRC in the keystream, but SSRC collisions are possible, and when two SSRCs share a master key their keystreams are identical over the overlapping part of the sequence number space. The security descriptions avoid keystream reuse by requiring unique master keys for the sender and the receiver.

Second, the ROC must be zero when each SSRC starts sending, so there is no concept of a late joiner in these security descriptions. Third, the initial SEQ should be chosen within the range 0 to 2^15-1, which avoids ambiguity when packets are lost at the start of the session; otherwise a source might pick a high sequence number and, if the first packets were lost up to the point the sequence number wraps, the receiver might not recognise that its ROC needs to be incremented.

Because of these constraints, unicast SRTP crypto contexts can be established without negotiating SSRC values. The RFC recommends an approach called late binding: the SSRC in a packet is bound to the crypto context when the packet arrives rather than when the description is exchanged. The context is first identified as a wildcard SSRC together with the local receive address and port, and when the first packet arrives with a given SSRC the context for that SSRC is instantiated. If media packets are authenticated, the authentication must succeed or the context is not created; if they are not authenticated, the context is created automatically, which invites easy denial of service and is not recommended.

When several SSRCs or several RTP sessions share the crypto parameters, an application that shares a master key among them must replace the master key when the aggregate number of packets across all the SSRCs approaches 2^31 packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Each stream of media is numbered, and the receiver keeps a count of how many packets it has seen so it can spot a replayed one. The specification fixes that count at zero when the session starts and asks for the first sequence number to be low, so that lost packets at the start cannot confuse the receiver.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Like all SDP messages, messages containing security descriptions are conveyed in an encapsulating application protocol such as SIP or MGCP, and it is that protocol's job to protect them. The RFC states that it is required that the application invoke its own security mechanisms, such as secure multiparts like S/MIME, or use a lower layer service such as TLS or IPsec, and that this service must provide strong message authentication, payload encryption and effective replay protection.

Replay protection is needed against an attacker who can intercept messages and deliver copies of them, causing the recipient to process a message twice; the attack is worse when the duplicated recipient sends a duplicate reply. Replay protections are not found in S/MIME or PGP/MIME, so they need to be added by the application protocol. Three common ways are to place a sequence number in the message, to use a timestamp, or for the receiver to keep a hash of the message to compare with incoming messages, usually with a replay window and a table of previous messages.

On the media side, an SRTP encryption service is misconfigured when two or more media streams are encrypted using the same keystream of AES blocks. When senders and receivers share derived session keys, SRTP requires the SSRCs to make their keystreams unique, and an SSRC collision drastically weakens the encryption while the identical keystreams are in use; an attacker could collect SRTP and SRTCP messages and wait for a collision. This attack is avoided entirely when each media stream has its own unique master key in both the send and the receive direction, which is what restricting these descriptions to unicast point-to-point streams achieves.

Finally, the signalling must be protected too. In most cases the crypto attribute and its parameters are vulnerable to denial of service when carried in an unauthenticated SDP message, and sometimes the integrity or confidentiality of the RTP stream can be compromised: an attacker who sets the UNENCRYPTED parameter for the SRTP stream in an offer could make the answerer send unencrypted SRTP. Failing to encrypt an SDP message that carries an inline master key renders the SRTP service useless in practically all circumstances, and failing to authenticate it renders the service useless in most practical applications. Where the SDP message passes through intermediate systems that inspect parts of it, IPsec or TLS should not be used to protect the description, because those terminate at each intermediate system; the attributes should be protected end to end so that the intermediate system can neither modify the description nor reach the keying material, and MIME secure multiparts are recommended for that case.
sections.plainLanguage: The rule is that the key must travel protected, and the description around it must be protected too, so that nobody can change the settings or read the key on the way. The RFC also warns against sharing one key between two streams, because that makes the encryption of both easy to break.

messages.label: OFFER

messages.note: Accepts exactly one crypto line and returns the answerer's own key.

items.title: KDR
items.text: Key derivation rate: a power of two from 2^1 to 2^24.

items.title: UNENCRYPTED_SRTP
items.text: The SRTP payloads are not encrypted.

items.title: UNENCRYPTED_SRTCP
items.text: The SRTCP payloads are not encrypted.

items.title: UNAUTHENTICATED_SRTP
items.text: The SRTP messages are not authenticated. Not recommended.

items.title: FEC_ORDER
items.text: Whether error correction is applied before or after SRTP.

items.title: FEC_KEY
items.text: Separate master keys for an error correction stream elsewhere.

items.title: WSH
items.text: A hint for the size of the replay protection window; 64 is the minimum.
